transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I guess... it's just that I feel like I’ve got this motor humming right under my skin whenever I’m supposed to sit still. Like, if I'm in a morning staff meeting at the building, or sitting through those church event briefings. 

Actually, speaking of the church, we just had this huge spring festival last weekend. Pastor Dave brought his smoker out, and he makes a decent brisket, but honestly, he goes way too heavy on the hickory wood. I used to smoke meats a lot back when I lived down south in my twenties—you really gotta balance the wood with the rub, you know? My buddy Earl and I actually thought about opening a food truck once, but the permits were a nightmare. 

But, uh... wait, why did I bring that up? Oh, right, the briefings. Yeah, so when I'm supposed to be listening in those meetings, I just can't stay in the chair. I end up shifting around constantly, or I'll just stand up in the back, or I find some excuse to go check the supply closets or grab a broom so I can just move around. It's just getting to be a lot, I guess.
Do you also find yourself feeling restless or needing to move around in other situations, like when you're watching TV, reading, or trying to relax at home?

Yeah, it’s not just at work. Even when I’m supposed to be taking it easy... like, my wife and I like to go fishing, or sometimes she drags me down to the community center for bingo. Which, by the way, the caller they have for bingo, Jimmy? He’s got this microphone that constantly feeds back. Just this high-pitched squeal every five minutes. Drives me crazy. I told him he needs to check the grounding on his PA system or get a new cable. Being the building guy at my job, I deal with the AV setups in our auditorium all the time, and just last month I had to completely tear apart our soundboard because someone spilled a whole cherry soda on it. Sticky, sugary mess everywhere. Took me three hours with rubbing alcohol and a box of Q-tips just to unstick the volume sliders. People really have no respect for expensive equipment, you know? 

But, uh... anyway, relaxing. Right. So even at bingo or out on the boat, I just can't seem to be quiet and enjoy it. I'll catch myself tapping the table, or messing with my dauber and pencil, or I end up talking way too loud. Out on the water, I'm always digging around in my tackle box, reorganizing the lures, retying knots when I don't even need to. My wife gets so aggravated because she says I'm making too much of a racket and scaring all the bass away. It's just really hard for me to just... sit there and do nothing.
Do you find it hard to focus or stay concentrated on tasks, even when you're trying to pay attention?

Focusing? No, not really. I mean, if I'm doing a task, I can pay attention just fine. Like when I'm buffing the floors in the main atrium at work. I run this heavy-duty industrial rotary buffer, and you really have to be zeroed in on the pads you're using. You can't just slap a green pad on there for a daily polish, it'll strip the wax right down to the linoleum. You gotta use the white ones. 

But my supervisor, Gary, he ordered a whole pallet of the green ones last month by mistake. Just completely botched the purchase order. Gary means well, but he used to manage an auto parts store before they hired him for facilities, and I honestly don't think he knows the first thing about commercial floor care. Actually, speaking of auto parts, I had to replace the alternator in my Chevy last night. Took me four hours because the mounting bolts were completely rusted shut. Had to soak them in WD-40 and just wail on them with a rubber mallet for a good twenty minutes before they even budged. 

But, uh... sorry, what were we talking about? Concentrating, right. Yeah, no, I don't have any trouble focusing on what I'm doing. If I've got a job to do, I stay on it. It's really just the sitting around in chairs doing nothing that gets to me.

Have you ever experienced sudden episodes where you feel intense fear or discomfort that comes out of nowhere, like your heart starts racing, you feel short of breath, or like something terrible is going to happen?

Panic attacks? No, I don't think I've ever had anything like that. My heart doesn't race unless I'm doing something strenuous, you know? Like last week, I was helping my neighbor, Tom, haul this old cast-iron bathtub out of his bathroom. He’s doing a full remodel, tearing it down to the studs. He found this beautiful subway tile on clearance at the home improvement store, but I told him, you gotta make sure you use the right grout, or it’s gonna look terrible in a year. The pre-mixed stuff is garbage. You really want to get the dry powder and mix it yourself. 

Tom didn't listen, of course. He never does. He’s the kind of guy who thinks he can learn everything from a five-minute YouTube video. Like the time he tried to wire his own ceiling fan and ended up blowing the breaker for half his house. I had to go over there at ten o'clock at night with my multimeter to figure out what he crossed. Turns out he wired the hot straight to the ground. Could have burned the place down.

But, uh... anyway. No, no sudden fear or anything like that. Just the restlessness, really.
When did you first start noticing these feelings of restlessness or needing to move around a lot? Was this something you experienced even as a child, like before you were 12 years old?

Yeah, oh yeah, this goes way back. I remember getting in trouble back in grade school all the time for popping out of my seat, talking over the teacher, rushing ahead before the directions were even finished. My mother used to say I acted like I was wound too tight, even as a little kid. She was always trying to get me to burn off energy. 

She put me in Little League, actually. Played shortstop. I was pretty good, too, but I couldn't stand standing out in the field waiting for something to happen. Our coach, Mr. Henderson, he was this old guy who chewed tobacco and always wore these bright red suspenders. He drove this beat-up Ford pickup truck that always smelled like wet dog because he brought his golden retriever, Buster, everywhere. Buster was a great dog, but he had this habit of stealing the baseballs during practice and burying them out past the outfield fence. We spent half our practice time just digging up baseballs. They'd be all covered in mud and slobber, and Mr. Henderson would just wipe them off on his pants and throw them back in the bucket. You don't see coaches like that anymore, you know? Nowadays everything has to be so sanitized and official. 

But, uh... what was I saying? Oh, right, being a kid. Yeah, I was definitely like this before I was 12. Always getting up, always talking out of turn. My mom said I was like a motor that wouldn't shut off.

There is no evidence of panic attacks or difficulty concentrating on tasks, which rules out F41.0 (Panic Disorder). Symptoms are consistent with ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation.

inference_history.note: The patient describes restlessness and an inability to sit still, particularly in structured settings like meetings, which points toward symptoms consistent with ADHD (F90.0). The narrative also includes a degree of anxiety (e.g., restlessness, avoidance of sitting still) which could suggest Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.0). Additionally, the patient shows some mild depressive symptoms (e.g., frustration, feeling overwhelmed) which could indicate a mild depressive episode (F32.0). No definitive exclusions are made at this stage.

F32.0 was ruled out as the patient does not endorse symptoms of a major depressive episode such as low mood, anhedonia, changes in sleep/appetite, or feelings of worthlessness. The patient remains focused on tasks when engaged in activity, which is inconsistent with the inattentive presentation of ADHD (F90.0), but still meets criteria for hyperactivity/impulsivity. Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.0) remains plausible due to persistent restlessness, but there is no clear evidence of excessive worry or anxiety. No new disorder was added.
